title: The explainer that earns your trust
goal: Adapt an explanation to different readers without changing the underlying facts.
explanation: An analogy can make a topic memorable while quietly introducing a misconception. Start from a small source you can verify. Ask for a concrete example and a boundary for every analogy. Then answer a transfer question without reading the generated explanation.
sampleInput: Source facts: In a conventional computer, a bit has value 0 or 1. Quantum computation uses qubits and carefully controlled operations. Measuring a qubit gives an outcome; quantum computers do not simply try every answer and hand over all results. This is a beginner sketch, not a complete account.
prompt: Using only these facts, explain the topic first to a beginner and then to a history student. Use one analogy in each version, label where the analogy breaks, and include one check question. Do not introduce claims about guaranteed speedups or say a qubit is literally a spinning coin.
workedExample: A history-student analogy might compare different ways of organizing a calculation, then explicitly say historical armies or governments do not model quantum physics. A version that says “it computes every answer at once so all problems are instant” fails.

steps.title: Choose a verified source
steps.text: Use the supplied sketch or a short authoritative reference. List three facts that must survive both versions.

steps.title: Request two audiences
steps.text: Keep the source fixed. Change only the audience and analogy instructions.

steps.title: Audit the analogies
steps.text: Underline the useful comparison and circle any statement that treats the comparison as literal physics.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.text: Close the outputs and explain the three facts in your own words. Answer the check question.

steps.title: Repair one misconception
steps.text: Ask for a shorter explanation that removes the misleading analogy while preserving the fact.

checks: Both audience versions preserve the source’s three core facts.
Each analogy includes an explicit limitation.
Your own teach-back answers a new question rather than copying the output.
commonMistakes: Treating simpler wording as automatically more accurate.
Using a fluent analogy as a substitute for a reliable source.
offline: Write the two explanations yourself and have a reader identify where each analogy fails.
reflection: Which explanation helped you answer a new question, not just remember a phrase?

evidence.title: Keep the build
evidence.detail: Save your original input, exact prompt and resulting artifact. Both audience versions preserve the source’s three core facts.

evidence.title: Show what you tested
evidence.detail: Record a pass/fail result and evidence for every check below. Each analogy includes an explicit limitation.

evidence.title: Explain a limitation
evidence.detail: Write what changed after one deliberate revision and name a remaining failure mode. Treating simpler wording as automatically more accurate.
